title: Start bars and columns at zero, keep one scale per axis, and size circles by area.
rule: Draw an amount at its true size. Bars and columns start at zero, because a reader compares their lengths. A line may start above zero when the change is the point, with the axis labeled where it starts.

Each axis keeps one scale, so two measures take two panels side by side rather than a second axis on the right. A circle that stands for an amount takes its area from the value, so its radius grows with the square root of the value. A line or band whose width stands for an amount, as in a network or a flow, takes one unit across the whole drawing, with a key, so twice the width means twice the amount.

text: Readers judge a bar by its length before they read its number. Cut the axis at 55 percent and 1992’s 67.7 percent stands 3.7 times as tall as 1996’s 58.4, for a gap of 9.3 points.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the chart system our founder and editor approved in November 2026

builders: The kit draws every bar and column from zero and fails a circle not sized by area; scale may set a line’s range, never a bar’s.

specs.label: Bars and columns
specs.value: From a zero line drawn at the baseline weight

specs.label: A line
specs.value: May start above zero, with the axis labeled at its start

specs.label: Two measures
specs.value: Two panels on two scales, side by side

specs.label: Circles
specs.value: Area in proportion to the value, so the radius follows its square root

specs.label: Widths
specs.value: One unit for every line and band in the drawing, with a key; a line too thin to see at that unit drawn as a hairline, which the key names

correct.caption: From zero, each column keeps its true size: the highest share, 67.7 percent in 1992, stands about 16 percent taller than the lowest, 58.4 percent in 1996.
correct.alt: Columns from a zero line. In every presidential year from 1980 to 2024, between 58 and 68 percent of citizens 18 and over reported voting.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.4. The axis starts at 55 percent, so 1992’s column stands 3.7 times as tall as 1996’s for a gap of 9.3 points.
failure.alt: Failure case: do not publish. The same columns on an axis that starts at 55 percent, so 1992’s column stands 3.7 times as tall as 1996’s.
